doc.title: Rashied Ali and Henry Grimes interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 30, 2009

title: Witnessing Army integration at Camp Pickett
summary: Ali recalls the Army desegregating overnight, the fights that followed, equal pay, and the band staying calm.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Was the service integrated at that time?
No. I was in the Army when they integrated. I was there. You know, I mean, you know they integrated the whole Army in 24 hours.

They just went like, you know, like we lived on post, we lived this part of the post and all the white soldiers lived on that side of the post. Right? And we were the black outfit with all white officers and no black officers. And when I saw a black officer it was like wow, there’s a black captain, can you believe this? I mean we was like amazed. Because we never seen a black officer. And one day the Master Sergeant marched us all out, marched us all out, and they did the same thing across the tracks with the white guys, and then they called names, right? They called names. And they’d say okay you guys fall out over here and you guys fall out over here, then they just meshed them. Anybody just went together, and then we went back into our barracks and we integrated. Just like that.
And how did people feel about it?
Oh man we had more fights than you can believe.

Oh people would be saying the “N” word and people would be saying the “C” word and they’d be making mistakes and you know just this went on for quite a while. But it got okay, you know, it got okay. But it took a while. It took a while for us to adjust to each other. Because we would just say things that we were used to saying and then go uhh — and then they’d go bang. You know, it was like pretty rough. But it was really cool. I mean it really turned out good and in the band, we didn’t have no problems in the band because we had a sergeant who didn’t take any stuff at all. And it was really cool. I mean I was there when they integrated the Army. The United States Army. I was on the scene. Yeah. That was something else.
Was there any discrepancy in the pay you got between the white and the black soldiers?

Everybody got the same benefits. Everybody got the same everything. There wasn’t no thing like that. It was just segregated, that’s all. And they desegregated the Army, just like, I mean the whole United States Army they did it like that. I guess they did, because, I don’t know, they did it to us. And we were in Camp Pickett Virginia when that happened.
That was in 1953 I believe it was.
